author: Hassan Aslam Shad
headline: Senior Corporate Lawyer at Al Hejailan Law | Cross-Border M&A & Family Office Advisory | Harvard Law School LL.M.
text:
Foreign investors of every category have been able to buy shares directly on the Main Market of the Saudi Exchange since 1 February 2026. This followed the Capital Market Authority's decision to remove the Qualified Foreign Investor regime and discontinue its swap agreement framework.

The change marks a major step in a process the Authority began more than a decade ago. Ownership limits remain in place for now. A non-resident foreign investor may not hold 10% or more of a listed company, and aggregate foreign ownership is capped at 49%, although foreign strategic investors fall outside both limits.

Anyone with strategic intentions therefore needs to think about structure as well as access. Building a significant position brings disclosure obligations as the holding grows, and the strategic investor route carries its own conditions, including a minimum holding period of two years.

The Authority has said these limits are under review, so investors planning larger positions should follow its announcements closely.

headline: Founder @ Kara Motors Limited | Master of Civil Engineering | Project Engineer | Graduate Certificate in Infrastructure Engineering Manageme
text:
MENA startup funding fell 96% in a single month this past October — just $40 million raised across the entire region, the lowest total in a long while, with no big deals anywhere. And yet one Saudi company alone still pulled in almost a third of that.

That company is Autobia, a Saudi B2B platform that connects auto-parts retailers and wholesalers with verified suppliers, handling the sourcing, fulfilment, and logistics in between. On October 11, it closed a $12 million Series A led by Artal Capital, with Aljazira Capital and Saudi Aramco's venture arm, Wa'ed Ventures, also putting money in. It's the company's second round since launching in 2021 — it raised $2.5 million in seed funding back in 2023. Beyond the marketplace itself, Autobia also lets retailers buy inventory on flexible payment terms and manage their own customers' payments through licensed financing providers, which is really the harder, less glamorous problem in this industry: most parts businesses live or die on cash flow, not just on finding stock.

Saudi Arabia brought in $18.8 million of October's regional total, and Autobia's round alone made up close to two-thirds of that, enough for Wamda's own tracker to call autotech the single most-funded sector in the region that month.

Investors pulled back almost everywhere else in the region this month, and still backed a company solving something as unglamorous as parts logistics and working capital — a sign this is a real, provable pain point, not a trend bet.

author: Anas Ansar
headline: Managing Partner - Inaya Advisory
text:
HUMAIN, Saudi Arabia's state AI company, plans to launch a venture capital fund of more than $10 billion before the end of this year.

Saudi Arabia's sovereign fund, PIF, set it up in May 2025. On 1 November, Aramco paid $2.6 billion in cash for 49% of it, and PIF kept the other 51%.

The fund will invest in AI companies in the US, Europe and Asia, with offices in the US, Saudi Arabia, France and the UK. 

Its CEO, Tareq Amin, has said it could end up bigger than the $10 billion first announced in 2025. HUMAIN has already shown how it writes checks: $3 billion into xAI in February, which Amin calls "a home run".

The money comes with one condition. 

Companies it backs must run part of their computing on Saudi data centers or move staff to the Kingdom. 

"We don't do passive investments," Amin said. That is Vision 2030 in a single clause: the check goes to America, and part of the work comes home.

For a US AI company raising this year, the first meeting with HUMAIN will be about where your compute runs. Have that answer ready before you talk valuation.


Sources: Semafor, 3 Sep 2026 · Fortune, 9 Sep 2026 · Aramco / PIF, 1 Nov 2026

text:
MENA startup funding fell 96% in a single month this past October — just $40 million raised across the entire region, the lowest total in a long while, with no big deals anywhere. And yet one Saudi company alone still pulled in almost a third of that.

That company is Autobia, a Saudi B2B platform that connects auto-parts retailers and wholesalers with verified suppliers, handling the sourcing, fulfilment, and logistics in between. On October 11, it closed a $12 million Series A led by Artal Capital, with Aljazira Capital and Saudi Aramco's venture arm, Wa'ed Ventures, also putting money in. It's the company's second round since launching in 2021 — it raised $2.5 million in seed funding back in 2023. Beyond the marketplace itself, Autobia also lets retailers buy inventory on flexible payment terms and manage their own customers' payments through licensed financing providers, which is really the harder, less glamorous problem in this industry: most parts businesses live or die on cash flow, not just on finding stock.

Saudi Arabia brought in $18.8 million of October's regional total, and Autobia's round alone made up close to two-thirds of that, enough for Wamda's own tracker to call autotech the single most-funded sector in the region that month.

Investors pulled back almost everywhere else in the region this month, and still backed a company solving something as unglamorous as parts logistics and working capital — a sign this is a real, provable pain point, not a trend bet.

text:
The biggest schedule risk on capital projects here is not labour, and it is not the contractor. It is a transformer.

Large power transformers are running around 128 weeks on average, more than 160 weeks for substation units, and up to four years for the largest high-voltage machines, according to Wood Mackenzie’s survey data. Medium-voltage switchgear sits roughly 50 per cent above 2019 prices.

And the queue is no longer formed only by industrial projects. Saudi data center load reached 467 MW in the first quarter of this year, up from 68 MW in 2021 (MCIT, May 2026), and the announced pipeline is an order of magnitude larger. HUMAIN alone has set out 6.6 GW by 2034, and the Al-Saad campus tendered this year covers 24 square kilometer's in six one-gigawatt plots.

Read the electrical scope of one of those campuses and it looks familiar: 380/132/33 kV networks, 500 and 200 MVA substations, a 2,000 MVA bulk supply point. That is the same equipment, from the same factories, that a refinery tie-in or a new district needs. A data center in Riyadh is now in the same queue as a petrochemical expansion in Jubail.

Three things follow.
▪ The long-lead item is no longer inside the schedule. It is the schedule. On a growing number of projects the transformer purchase order sets the completion date, not construction.
▪ Procurement starts before the design is finished. Reserve the slot, then engineer into it. Uncomfortable, and now the cost of entry.

→ The Sovereign Engine: Aramco printed SR 379.02B, carrying 95.7% of total sector profits.
→ The Disruption Winners: Supply bottlenecks propelled Bahri up 586.7% and swung Petro Rabigh from a SR 3.29B loss to a SR 6.7B profit.
→ The Margin Bloodbath: Oilfield services got crushed—Arabian Drilling profits collapsed 90.6% (SR 6.9M) and ADES Holding dropped 23% (SR 459.8M).

A rising macro tide in Riyadh does not lift every balance sheet. Foreign companies and allocators who enter the Gulf without segment-level intelligence get burned on execution.

text:
A customer in Riyadh pays the same price for the same machine, whether it was built in Europe or in the Kingdom. What changes is who keeps the difference.

The document below follows EUR 100 of export revenue from a European plant to that customer, in our model's base case. Freight and handling take 4.0. Duty takes 5.2. A plant in Saudi Arabia keeps most of both: 108.1 instead of 100, after delivery inside the country.

Across our three scenarios, that is 6.6 % to 10.2 % more revenue per unit for a European manufacturer. It is real, and it is the smaller lever. The larger one sits on the cost side, and it depends on where the manufacturer produces today.

The calculator lets you set freight, duty and delivery for your own product. The link is in the first comment.
